analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Your arguments next in Kentucky against Graham. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. After briefly summarizing the facts of this case, I intend to explain to this court precisely why the court below erred in its construction of Hutto v. Finney, and why in any event, United States Code 42, United States Code section 1988 provided no authority for the award of attorney's fees in this particular case. And that indicates that the police were violating the policies of the state of Kentucky. And perhaps most importantly in this case, the district court dismissed the state of Kentucky as a party defendant in the virtue of the 11th Amendment. Kentucky? Kentucky? Counsel, if this lawsuit had been on the state side in the Commonwealth courts, would the Commonwealth be a proper party defendant? Your Honor, we would contend, had that occurred, that under 1983 Kentucky would not be a proper party defendant. And secondly, there is no proof to indicate that the state of Kentucky was responsible for the policies that were followed by the police in this particular occasion. Of course, the second state of Kentucky doesn't go to whether it could be a defendant anyway, but you would say no under 1983? Your Honor, that would be our contention. You are correct. The 11th Amendment, of course, would not apply in state court. Our point is that the state of Kentucky has prevailed in this case on absolutely every aspect on the merits, yet the state was saddled with the attorney's fees. Now, it's our contention that although the plaintiffs were in fact the prevailing parties as to the remaining defendants in this case, they were not the prevailing party as to the Commonwealth of Kentucky, and the court erred by awarding attorney's fees under that section in 1988. The plaintiffs could have obtained attorney's fees in this particular case from the remaining defendants, but they bargained away those rights in their settlement negotiations. Now, the second issue that I would like to present to the court today is concerned with the 11th Amendment, and it likewise is a very narrow issue as well. This court has recognized that the 11th Amendment bars a suit in federal court against a state by a citizen of the same state or other states. Now, in this particular case, the trial court recognized this principle and accordingly dismissed the state of Kentucky. But this court has also recognized that under the fiction and ex parte young, a court may award prospective relief against a state officer in his official capacity in joining him from carrying out a policy of the state or a state statute which runs foul of the Constitution. If the court does that, if the court does that, is to award that kind of prospective relief, this court has then recognized in HUD or VIFINI that it is permissible to award an attorney's fees ancillary to that type of prospective relief. And the reason for that is because the state is, in fact, for all purposes, if for all practical purposes, the party in the case, although not named as the party. And this court has not held likewise with regard to retrospective relief against a state. This court has never held that 1983 abrogates the 11th Amendment so as to provide retrospective relief against the state. The state of Kentucky would submit that that would apply likewise to 1988. Essentially, what we are saying is that an attorney's fee has no greater status than the award on the merits that it is ancillary to. And in this case, there was no award on the merits against the state of Kentucky. It was prohibited by the 11th Amendment. The only award at all was against the remaining defendants in their individual capacities. Since there was no award on the merits against the state of Kentucky in this case, then an attorney's fee ancillary is prohibited in the case. May I ask one more question? Your brief recites that there were $64,870-some dollars of costs, of which $58,000 were attorney's fees, so about $10,000 in costs that are not attorney's fees. What is your position with respect to the costs, not the fees? Your Honor, my position would be the same as the attorney's fees, but I'm afraid that we did not appeal that part of the decision. I see you only appealed the fee parts of the other. Your Honor, that is correct. For these reasons, I submit that the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit should be reversed, and a reversal according to the arguments that I've made would require no modification of the existing case law of this court. Thank you. Mr. Lowry. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. I think it would be helpful at the outset to briefly review the two statutes that are involved in this appeal. The first, of course, being 1983. It simply provides that every person who subjects or causes to be subjected another person of a violation of his constitutional rights shall be liable to that person in an action in law, suit in equity, or other proper proceeding. State. How does the state fit into that? How does the state fit into that statute? Judge, I guess the best you could say was that counsel named them improvidently. Probably the worst you could say is they named them ignorantly. Actually, the truth falls somewhere in between. We were concerned at that point in the case that it might be necessary to make a record, that there might be an issue of the right to name a state, that the efficacy of the 11th Amendment could even be an issue. And so, to make sure that the state of Kentucky received full notice, we named them as a party. Now, the district court, we take no issue at all with the action of the district court in dismissing them. But we do call to the attention of the court that the state... Well, if they had never been joined... If they'd never been joined... If they'd never been joined, could a fee be assessed against them? Yes, sir. Hutto says, and the Senate reports and House reports say that a fee may be assessed against the state, whether or not named as a party. Now, that's pure Hutto, as well as Mayor against Gagne. That is well settled law, as far as I know, and is not disputed, as far as I know. So we did name the state. We did think that there might be... It might be desirable to make a record. And as it turned out, it was not, because the matter was settled, and that issue was never raised on appeal. The other part of the statute that I'm referring to here, of course, is 1988, which simply provides that anyone who vindicates constitutional rights under 83, and is a prevailing party, shall be awarded a reasonable attorney's fee as part of the cost. Now, as a very preliminary and basic response to the argument that only injunctive relief, retrospective relief, will trigger the workings of 1988, I simply look at the wording of 1983. And had I been requested by Congress to sit down and help them draft an all-inclusive provision, one not restricted to retrospective relief, but one that included a broad arsenal of legal remedies available to those whose constitutional rights were violated, I don't believe I could improve on this language. I was taught, in an action that law means to go into court and ask for damages. And a suit in equity is a suit where you undertake to get injunctive relief. We think it's self-evident as far as the wording itself of Section 1983 is concerned. The real question, it seems to me, is what was the intent of Congress in enacting 1988? Did Congress intend to make it restrictive? Did they intend to make it all inclusive? Did they intend to amend the 11th Amendment? Well? You should bring that in. All right, sir. As far as the 11th Amendment is concerned, we're faced with Edelman, the Edelman case. The Edelman case wasn't, that was a case, not brought under 1983. There was no attorney's fee involved in Edelman, but it was a case in which injunctive relief was approved. The 11th Amendment didn't bar injunctive relief, but it did bar retroactive damages. Then comes along Fitzpatrick v. Bitschner, written by the same justice, of course. But it cast, in my mind, grave doubt on Edelman. It held just the opposite. Now, it was a different statute, of course. There was a Title VII statute, I believe, involved in Fitzpatrick. But Fitzpatrick awarded attorney's fees. It awarded injunctive relief. It awarded damages. Then you come along with Mayor against Jagney that says if the 11th Amendment ever barred suits of this nature, it was destroyed by Congress in an act in 1988. There's a concurring opinion in Hutto that suggests that that is a burning question now. But in my view, it's a question that does not have to be reached in this case, because here we're dealing with attorney's fees and attorney's fees only, which are different. Attorney's fees are different, because Hutto says, and it takes about two pages to say it, attorney's fees are not damages. That is where the attorney general confuses and conflicts his argument. Attorney concede that the state was not a proper party here. On the merits, yes, sir. Then suppose they'd mistakenly, inadvertently, included the state of New York as a party defendant, and then the court promptly dismissed them. Could you collect fees against the state of New York? No, sir. I think I... That's the difference. I beg your pardon? That's the difference between Kentucky and New York in this setting and on this record. In my judgment, Your Honor, our name in the state of Kentucky was like suing the West Wind, with the law being as it was then. All that required was a motion to dismiss. If no motion had been made and some type of default action in the first place, I don't think a district court could be found in this country that would enter one, at least they're no worse off... I can see you collect one. Well, that's true. At least they're no worse off by being named than they would be if they were not even named. But how can you say you prevailed against them if you concede that you had nothing against them on the merits and the claim was dismissed? Because we never had any standing to proceed against them. That was not a matter in issue. You know, my question is, how can you say that you, in order to get a tuning case under Section 98 and 98, you have to show that you, as against the state of Kentucky, are the prevailing party? Yes, sir. How do you show that? In the case of a state, since you cannot name a party, the way you become a prevailing party is to name a policymaking official and sue him in his official capacity. As recently as January, Brandon against Holt, decided to this court, said in three recent cases, we have suggested that a person becomes liable to his entity if he's named in his official capacity. We now make that point explicit. Yes, but you didn't sue these people in the official capacity. Oh, yes, sir. We sued Commissioner Brandenburg in his official capacity, and that is not contested. But he was not defended by the state of Kentucky. No, sir, he was not. The state of Kentucky took the unusual position in this case that after the horse was out of the stable and after the attorney general in an independent investigation found out all these wrongdoings that cited in this brief, they decided that the best way out of the case was just to abandon Commissioner Brandenburg, which is what they attempted to do. We think, ineffectually, we don't think it's possible for a state to abandon a policymaking official. Did you allege in your complaint in which you sued Brandenburg that he was the authorized agent of the state of Kentucky? Oh, yes, sir. And as a matter of fact, we have cited the Kentucky revised statutes that spell out his authority. He was the number one-ranking police officer in the state of Kentucky. The state goes out and raises a lynch mob and then lynches somebody. Do you think you can recover some either damages or fees against the state? Yes, sir, I do. By assuring the governor in his official capacity, he being an official... Don't you also have to prove that when he performed the lynching function, the lynch mob, he was acting in his official capacity, not outside his official capacity? Judge, in my view, this is not a scope-of-employment type of situation. The governor is official policy. Commissioner Brandenburg is official policy. That is why there is not going to be this huge floodgate of litigation that's been referred to by the amicus. Well, on your theory, if the governor shoots somebody in a duel, then it's the act of the state, too, isn't it? The state becomes liable. The state says that's not true. I beg your pardon? In some states, you can't sue the governor. Well... I give you the citation, volume one of the Arkansas Reports. Well, then I don't know what you do. Page one, you can't sue them. I will take it that you could under a 1983 in federal court in that state, however. They didn't have 1988 then. Right, sir. Right. When Arkansas started. Right. I'm only referring to that situation. Why they weren't included. Why they weren't what? Why they were included, other than that you wanted to do just what you're doing now, argue for a cleanest fee. Out of the state. Well, may I say this. May I cite the court to answer that question? An opinion, I believe, by Justice Powell, in which he pointed out that the request for attorney's fees is a uniquely separable inquiry that cannot even commence until after the marriage is over. There's not a prevailing party until the marriage are over. Once the merits are over, for the first time, now can be addressed the question of attorney's fees. Is that written in the context of a case where the party plaintiff did not prevail against the party against whom fees are sought? Judge, I won't quote the facts precisely, but I say the concept that the Commonwealth of Kentucky was a prevailing party simply because they were erroneously at that time, and assuming the 11th Amendment continues to be in full efficacy. Well, how can you get attorney's fees for being, quote, erroneous? We get attorney's fees, Your Honor, by prevailing. You put them in, it was a mistake, right? As it turned out, it might not have been a mistake. But was it? Yes, we'll say it was a mistake. Have you given me any other case where any lawyer officially got a fee for making a mistake? Not for making a mistake. The fee entitlement comes in this case by the actions of a policy-making state official, the commissioner of the Kentucky State Police, and I obtaining a settlement against him. If Kentucky had never been named as a party, you should, by naming the official, in his official capacity, you were entitled to fees against the state. Yes, sir. And you shouldn't be deprived of them because you made a mistake by naming the state initially. You say it better than I do, Judge. Yes, sir. That's my point. To get back to this retroactive retrospective, I'm reminded of an illustration that comes to my mind. Here's a commissioner of corrections. He puts ten prisoners per sale. He gives them a thousand calories a day. He deprives them medical attention. Hutto, all over. Is it a 1983 action? Yes. Would you be entitled to attorney's fees if you prevailed? Yes. Would you be entitled to retrospective relief? Yes. Now, same commissioner of corrections, same penitentiary, same prisoner even, and he overhears the two guards saying, we're going down and fix that guy for starting all this turmoil. And they go down and they beat the guard up. Retrospective relief? No. It's already over with. It's already happened. It's not an ongoing thing. But it's a constitutional violation. And in our view, Congress did not pick and choose. Congress didn't say, we want to crown certain amendments with an award of attorney's fees. If you hadn't settled, do you think you could have gotten an award for damages against the commissioner? Judgment representing the plaintiff, you always hope that. Yeah, but I mean, would there have been any legal barrier to getting a judgment against him in his official capacity? No, sir. No, sir. Well, do you think if you could have gotten that sort of a judgment in his official capacity, could you have collected it from the state of Kentucky? Oh, yes, sir. And that's exactly what we're trying to do here. Which of our cases support that rather surprising view? Brandon against Holt? Hutto against Finney? Well, Hutto against Finney and didn't involve retrospective damages. Well, Fitzpatrick against... What is Fitzpatrick against... No, I mean, all of the states deprive the states of their sovereign immunity. Oh, yes, sir. I know that. Well, so this is a 1983 suit, and you say that just by the simple mechanism of suing an official, in his official capacity, you can get a judgment for damages against the state. You don't do it that way. Well, you get a judgment against the official, in his official capacity, and then you collect it from the state. Then you ask the district judge to have a hearing on what you're entitled to. And you say that in that way you avoid the sovereign immunity of the state. Yes, sir. Because, judge, and the reason you do, the reason you do is that attorney's fees are not damages. Well, I'm talking about damages now. Well, no, sir. The state is still shielded from the award of damages. And so, and, and, and, so, but you still think you get a judgment against the official, in his official capacity? Yes, sir. Well, it wouldn't do you any good because you couldn't collect it from the state. Sorry? You couldn't collect it from the state. You'd have to collect it from him or no one. Well, I think you could collect it from the state. What if the legislature just refused to appropriate any money? What are you going to do, a levy on the state capitol? No, sir. I think the district court would order the state. Order the legislature? No, sir. Would order, in this case, a commissioner, the present commissioner of the state police, Hutto against Finney spells it out, the agency involved, the district court wouldn't have any problem. What you say is that the plaintiff cannot name the state as a party in the 1980 reaction, but it can name a state official in his official capacity, get an award of damages against him, and then go into the district court in a kind of supplemental proceeding, and the district court would order the state to pay the damages? Within its discretion. If the district court who's been sitting there and supervising this entire thing thinks the claim is spurious, if you've been... Well, then the Eleventh Amendment is really a matter of form, since there are very good ways of avoiding it, I tell you. No, sir, it's because, and if your Honor will refer to Hutto, Hutto takes about two pages saying that 1988 does not come under the Eleventh Amendment because attorney fees are not damages. Now, that distinction has to be made because... in Congress or any place under the sun that said that the Eleventh Amendment does not apply to 1988, except you. Now, name anything else, anybody else. All right, sir. Hutto against Fennig. Yes, sir. Certainly there's language in Hutto against Finney that might lend some support, perhaps, to your position, but it didn't involve retrospective damages, did it? No, ma'am, it didn't, but Fitzpatrick did. Fitzpatrick against Bixer did. But didn't Corey against White have something to say about getting relief directly from the state? I'm not familiar with that case, Your Honor. Yes, sir. Just to answer your questions, the Mayor case, Mayor against Jagney, says... Both Hutto and Mayor. Well, read me one of them, Mayor. All right, sir. Don't paraphrase, just read. I was going to get me that man's case, please. And I wanted to say that the 11th Amendment is not included in 1988, end of quote. I can find it, Judge. I'll read it to you. All right. All right, sir. And here I'm applying on page 662. Now, this is Lawyer's Edition, that I have a copy of here. I trust that won't cause problems. Lawyer's Edition, second. What case? Mayor against Jagney, if I pronounce it correctly. And I'm applying the U.S. citation is 438 U.S. 132. More, even if the 11th Amendment would otherwise present a barrier to an award of fees against the state, Congress was clearly acting within its power under Section 5 of the 14th Amendment in removing that barrier. Under Section 5, Congress may pass any legislation that's appropriate to enforce the guarantees of the 14th Amendment. A statute awarding attorney's fees to a person who prevails on a 14th Amendment claim for the 14th Amendment. Pardon my breathlessness. Falls within the category of appropriate legislation. It didn't say that the 15th Amendment was written out of it. You've got to consider the 11th Amendment. Well, I don't dispute it. That's what I asked you for, where it said that you couldn't consider the 11th Amendment. Yes, here's more language. Now, this is from Hutto, quoted in that case. This court has never viewed the 11th Amendment as barring such awards, even in suits between states and individual litigants. Now, that's another quotation from Hutto against Finney. This is where you deliberately put somebody in there solely for the purpose of getting council fees out of the state. Judge, not putting them in at that stage in the proceedings. You admitted you didn't mean to do it. You made a mistake. I don't think I made a mistake. I think I probably, well, I made a mistake in the long run in doing it. I knew what I was doing when I did it, and I think perhaps had I to do it over, I wouldn't have done it. But at that stage, I wasn't, Judge, at that point on the merits, they weren't liable for attorney's fees. They weren't liable at all for anything. They weren't liable on the merits. The question of attorney's fees only came up after the merits was over. Just to clarify it in my mind, your claim for fees would be precisely the same if you had never named the state as a defendant. Is that right? Yes, sir. That's exactly right. And I wanted to mention this Brandon against Holt case. In at least three recent cases arising under 1983, we plainly implied that a judgment against a public servant in his official capacity imposes liability on the entity that he represents, provided the court goes on, of course, the public entity received notice and an opportunity to respond. That doesn't solve your 11th Amendment problem, because there you're talking about the city of Memphis, were you now? You're talking about a city here. However, the three cases that the court relied on, two of them were a city and one was a state. The one in the state was Hutto against Vinnie? Yes, sir. What was it? I beg your pardon? How did the court divide in Hutto against Vinnie? Judge, I don't recall. It seems to me it was a divided court. Mr. Lowry, can I ask one other question? Yes, sir. Because there's some confusion in my mind about the difference between suing one in his official capacity and one in his individual capacity. Right. And you read the complaint clearly as saying you sued him in their official capacity. But may I direct your attention to the order in July of 82 when the individual defendants were dismissed and the district judge said that no claims for attorney's fees shall be made by any party plaintiff against any of the individual party defendants or the Kentucky State Police Legal Fund, a voluntary association. And as I understand, they weren't ever even a party to the lawsuit, were they? No, they were not. But does not that paragraph suggest that he thought they were being sued in their individual capacity? Well, I don't have the complaint in front of you, but I think we probably did sue them in their individual capacity. Truth in mind, your honor, most of these defendants were not policy-making officials. They were sergeants and patrolmen and they were this and that and the other day. Do you think the mere fact that you allege an officer is a policy-making official? That is sufficient to be an allegation that you're suing him in his official capacity? Yes, sir. Now, you have to go ahead and prove it. There wasn't much of a dispute about what responsibilities. And there's been no dispute in this case that he was a policy-making official. Any other? Thank you very much. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court, I will waive rebuttal unless this court has any questions. May I just ask, I don't know, maybe this is outlined because of that order, but could these fees have been recovered from the individual defendants in their individual capacities had they gotten a judgment on the merits for the amount of the settlement and then went in for fees and then the state takes a position. Now, would they have been able to get the same fee award from these individuals? Your Honor, our position is that they could get the fee awards, could have gotten the fee awards from the individuals, and I think we indicated earlier in the argument they had negotiated away those rights. They stipulated that away, is your view, from the settlement. Thank you, gentlemen. The case is submitted.
